newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge dismisses part of Fox News lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge dismisses part of Fox News lawsuit.

text.p: U.S. District Judge Jack Weinstein on Friday dismissed claims of fraud by Fox News Service against Time Warner Inc and transferred Fox's antitrust complaint to federal court in Manhattan, according to court papers provided by Time.

Granting a motion sought by Time in its cable television dispute with Fox, a unit of News Corp Ltd, Weinstein also dismissed Fox's claims of promissory estoppel. This involves a promise that is reasonably expected and, if broken, could be detrimental to the party who received the promise.
Weinstein ordered that the rest of Fox's complaint be transferred to federal court in Manhattan from federal court in Brooklyn, the court papers showed.

Fox had sought to get its all-news network included on Time's cable TV system in New York. When Time said it had no more space on its system, Fox sued, alleging that Time officials had reneged on oral assurances made to Fox executives.
News Corp said in a statment that it would appeal Weinstein's decision on the fraud claims.

"We disagree with the court's decision on our fraud and estoppel claim," it said. "The court recognized that there is substantial ground for differences of opinion on these claims and suggested an immediate appeal, which we intend to pursue."

On the fraud claims, Weinstein ruled, "The parties did participate in intensive and complex negotiations, but they never reached -- or even approached -- agreement on the essentials to a contractual relationship in this esoteric field."

He continued, "The cajolery, as well as the blandishments, honey phrases and assurances that are to be expected in major negotiations between parties of this sort in this media-entertainment field did not constitute fraud or promissory estoppel under the circumstances."

On the issue of which court should hear the antitrust claims, Weinstein ruled, "While the present venue appears to be proper, the case should be transferred for the convenience of the witnesses and the efficient operation of the courts..."
Fox contends that many Brooklyn residents were affected by Time's acquisition of Turner Broadcasting. Fox alleged antitrust violations after that deal.

Weinstein, in his ruling, said transferring the case to Manhattan from Brooklyn "would prevent a waste of time, energy, and money, and would also protect the parties, witnesses, and the public against unnecessary inconvenience and expense."

Time applauded Weinstein's rulings. It said in a statement, "We are obviously pleased with the (judge's) decision. We have maintained all along that Time Warner has acted entirely properly in dealing with Fox."
In its bid to get the Fox channel on the Time cable system, News Corp tried to move it to a channel operated by New York City.
New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani approved the move, but it raised a political uproar, and a judge ultimately blocked the plan.
